units.translation: And in my heart there is anxious turmoil about the king's return.
they hold the farthest region around the Maeotian lake.
around the stream of Pluto's passage.
and the dark depths around Tartarus.
they sing the wedding song around your bath and bed.
I hear the clatter of chariots around the city.
I revere the gods around the Nile.
Then, wretched, I wandered along your shores for sustenance; now around Cocytus—I am likely soon to prophesy.
around the shore of Cenaean Zeus.
having leapt in a bound around the setting of the Pleiades.
if not now, when shall we have around prayer (thus Seidler for ἀμφίλιταν)?
You have spoken a true account about the order of things.
With synizesis of the syllables ew in a senarius
See ἡβάω [to be in the prime of youth].
O friendly gods who deliver, standing around the city.
to be in the prime of youth
To cast a slavish yoke upon Hellas.
having cast a yoke upon the neck of the sea.
Let us go; for he has nets around his limbs.
I surround with a boundless net, as for fish.
Remember the net with which they first ensnared you.
assailed on all sides by weapons
assailed on all sides by weapons
Schol. πάντοθεν βαλλομένοις· ἢ ἀμφοτέρωθεν [struck from all sides; or from both sides].
they hurl jagged stones at the citizens assailed on both sides.
struck from all sides; or from both sides
I think they will not ambiguously utter a lament for the two brothers.
as being in doubt whether to be angry with the city.
with ambidextrous hands: those of the bow because each hand works in shooting. Aeschylus in Telephus (fr. 237).
name of a god, for whom the Amphidromia are celebrated
Amphidromus: Aeschylus in Semele (fr. 221) invented a new deity for the Amphidromia, as if he meant the god of birth.
[On fr. 66, to which Hermann wanted to introduce ἀμφίδρομον [running from both sides], see under the word αὐρίδρομος [running in the morning].]
amphidromos: it also means one who views or leads from each side, or who is able to rush, as Aeschylus in the Edonians (fr. 61).
see under the word running in the morning
to put on around, to clothe
to put on around, to clothe
Middle form αμφιέσασθαι [to have clothed oneself] to be clothed.
Epigram attributed to Aeschylus (fr. 449) in Anth. Pal. 7, 255
who once, wretched, clothed their limbs with Ossaean dust.
having passed the double-yoked headland common to both seas.
Schol. ὁ ποιήσων ἄμφω ἡμᾶς ἀναθηλῆσαι [the one who will make us both flourish again].
and when will Zeus, flourishing on both sides, lay his hand upon it?
